When Was It?

History, taught as a game. Put real events in order on a timeline — and get graded by how many years you missed by, because missing by 8 years and missing by 800 are different lessons. Then walk through two documented moments — a printing shop in the 1450s, a control room in 1969 — and make the choices the people there actually faced.

Era Journeys

Short trips through a documented moment. The history is the scenery; the choices teach how people actually lived and worked. Every factual claim carries a record note saying what it stands on — and where the record runs thin, the journey says so instead of inventing.

The Full Why

Why a game about when? Because chronology is the skeleton of history: strip the dates away and the stories float loose from their causes. Three layers, one tap down each.

Why chronology is the skeleton — tap to open

What it is: chronology is simply events in their true order, at their true distances. What it means: a cause must come before its effect, so order is the first test of any story about why something happened. If the “cause” happened later, the story is wrong no matter how good it sounds. What it could mean for you: distance matters as much as order. Two events 8 years apart shared a world — the same people, tools and news. Two events 800 years apart did not. That is why this game grades you in years missed, not just right or wrong: a near miss means your sense of the past's shape is nearly right, and the size of a miss tells you what to fix.

One honest wrinkle: there is no year zero. The calendar steps from 1 BCE straight to 1 CE, so a gap across that line is the two numbers added, minus one. Caesar's assassination (44 BCE) to Hastings (1066 CE) is 44 + 1066 − 1 = 1,109 years — and that is exactly how the game counts it.

Cause chains — this made that possible — tap to open
Cheap books: rag paper (cheaper than animal skin) + metal movable type + oil-based ink + the screw press → a Bible in months instead of a scribe's years → books cheap enough for townspeople → more readers → ideas that could not be un-printed. The printing journey above walks this chain station by station.
Steam: Newcomen's engine (1712) drained mines → deeper mines, cheaper coal → better engines → engines on wheels (1804) → railways → towns and clocks and timetables reorganised around the train. Each link is dated in the Making Things set.
Flight: a balloon over Paris (1783) → a powered aeroplane at Kitty Hawk (1903) → a solo ocean crossing (1927) → the sound barrier (1947) → a human in orbit (1961) → a footprint on the Moon (1969). From first powered flight to the Moon: 66 years — one long lifetime. Chronology is what lets you feel that speed.

A chain is a claim, and claims can be argued with — each link above is a documented date, but “made possible” is not “made inevitable”. People chose, funded, resisted and failed at every step. The chains show the skeleton; the journeys show the people hanging on it.

The honest shelf — how history gets argued about — tap to open

How a date earns its place in this game: somebody at the time wrote it down, or an object carries it — a dated charter, a ship's log, a notary's record, a newspaper, a flight transcript, a photograph with a mission clock in it. Dates that rest on documents like those are the only ones dealt as cards.

Famous dates deliberately left out, and why:

· Johannes Gutenberg's birth year — often printed as “c. 1400”, but no record of his birth survives. A guess in a costume is still a guess, so it is not a card. (His lawsuit of November 1455 is documented — that is why the printing journey can stand on it.)
· The invention of the wheel — it appears across a wide span of centuries and places; there is no single documented day or year to grade fairly.
· The founding of Rome, 753 BCE — a traditional date handed down by later writers, not a contemporary record. Tradition is labelled tradition here, never dealt as fact.
· The exact day Fleming saw his mould in September 1928 — the month is documented by his work and his 1929 paper; the famous single day is retold with more confidence than the record holds. The card says September 1928, and the game grades that event by its year.

How arguments get settled — or don't: new documents surface, old ones get re-read, and dating tools (tree rings, radiocarbon, eclipse records in chronicles) cross-check the paperwork. Where the specialists still disagree, this page prints the disagreement instead of picking a winner. If a date on this page is ever shown wrong by a better document, the honest move is to change the card — the record outranks the page.
